subChunks.title: Why Generics & Generic Classes

storyBeats.text: Eldrin shows you a pre-generics cauldron labelled Object cauldron. He drops in a fireball, a potion, and a boot — all accepted. When retrieving, he must guess what each item is and risks pulling out something unexpected.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Before generics, every container accepted anything. The chaos was spectacular and the crashes, catastrophic. Generics seal the cauldron: Cauldron<Potion> — potions only. The compiler enforces the contract.

storyBeats.label: Generic Box

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The T is a placeholder — a type variable. When you create Box<String>, every T inside becomes String. The compiler checks all usages against that contract.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a generic class Pair<A, B> with fields A first and B second, a constructor, and access via fields. Create a Pair<String, Integer> representing a wizard name and level. Print both.
guidedPractice.hint: Use public fields or getters. The type parameters A and B become the declared types of first and second.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why generics were introduced in Java. What problem do they solve compared to using Object references?

questions.prompt: What does the T represent in class Box<T>?
options: A type parameter — a placeholder for any type
The letter T as a String
A type that must extend Object
questions.answer: A type parameter — a placeholder for any type
questions.explanation: T is a type parameter — a placeholder replaced by an actual type when the class is instantiated, e.g. Box<String>.

questions.prompt: You can use a primitive type like int directly as a generic type parameter (e.g. Box<int>).
questions.explanation: Generic type parameters require reference types. Use Box<Integer> (the wrapper class). Java auto-boxes int ↔ Integer automatically.

subChunks.title: Bounded Types & Wildcards

storyBeats.text: Eldrin wants a spell that finds the more powerful of any two artefacts — but it must work for swords, potions, and scrolls alike.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A bounded type parameter says: I will work with any T, but only if T promises to be Comparable. It narrows the universe of accepted types to only those that can be meaningfully ordered.

storyBeats.label: Generic max

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Wildcards — the ? — are for when the caller dictates the type and you merely need to read or write. PECS: if a structure produces values for you, use extends; if you consume (add to) it, use super.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Write a generic static method max(T a, T b) where T extends Comparable<T> that returns the larger of the two. Test with two integers and two strings.
guidedPractice.hint: Use a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b — compareTo returns positive when a > b.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain bounded type parameters in Java generics. What does <T extends Comparable<T>> mean and why is it useful?

questions.explanation: "banana".compareTo("apple") is positive (b > a alphabetically), so the condition is false and b ("apple") is returned.

questions.prompt: You have a method that reads elements from a list and adds them to a total. Which wildcard is appropriate?
questions.explanation: When reading (producing values) from a list, use ? extends. This allows List<Integer>, List<Double> etc. — PECS: Producer Extends.
